1.goal: To name what she does today when she does not understand, and to hear once what this lesson gives her instead.
run: Read the question on screen with her. The Portuguese is under it.
Take the answer as it comes. Portuguese is fine here.
Say once what today gives her: a way to ask people to say it again.
exact: What today is: "Today you learn to ask people to say it again. People do this in every language."
If she says she just smiles and nods: "That works once. Today you get two sentences you can use every time."
1.expected: Some version of pointing, smiling, or handing over the phone. That is the honest starting point, and it is the one the lesson replaces.
1.support: If nothing comes, offer two: does she point at things, or does she hand over her phone?
1.challenge: Ask whether it has ever cost her something on a trip.
1.monitoring: Whether she describes a strategy or an avoidance. Both are useful; only one of them she can keep.
1.evidence: What she does today when she does not understand -- the before of this lesson.
1.transition: Move on when she has said how she manages today.

2.goal: To place the scene: the hotel of lesson 1, two people at the desk, three short questions.
run: Read the brief with her. The Portuguese is under it.
Confirm three things: there are three questions, they are short, and the answers are sentences she already has from lesson 1.
Do not say what the three questions are. That comes on the next screens.
2.expected: She connects it to lesson 1: same hotel, same booking, and she already has the answers. She names at least one sentence she can reuse.
2.support: If she looks worried, point at the last sentence of the brief -- the answers are hers already.
2.challenge: Ask her to say one of the lesson 1 sentences out loud, before anything has been asked of her.
2.monitoring: Whether lesson 1 comes back on its own, or has to be pointed at.
2.evidence: Whether the four sentences of lesson 1 survived a week.
2.transition: Move on when she has named at least one sentence she can reuse here.

3.goal: To have her guess what the desk will ask, before she hears any of it.
3.interaction: T-S, guessing out loud. Portuguese accepted.
run: There is no audio on this screen. The first play is on the next one.
Read the three questions on screen out loud with her, and ask for a guess on each.
Do not confirm and do not correct. These are hypotheses.
Accept Portuguese, and give the guess back in English so she hears it once.
exact: Giving a guess back in simple English: "So: your name, how many nights, and breakfast. Say it with me -- my name, how many nights, breakfast."
If nothing comes, three options: "Your name, the dates, or the price?"
3.expected: A guess for each of the three questions on screen. Name and nights usually come up; breakfast usually does not, and that is fine -- it is a guess.
3.support: Offer a few options and let her choose. Choosing is still risking.
3.challenge: Ask what she would say if she heard none of the three.
3.monitoring: Whether she guesses without being sure -- the second lesson in which that matters more than the answer.
3.evidence: Whether guessing is getting easier than it was in lesson 1.
3.transition: Move on when she has offered a guess for each of the three questions on screen.

4.goal: To recognize which questions were asked and how many people asked them. No answers yet.
run: Read the two questions on screen with her before you play anything.
Play the recording once. It is one file, with the three questions inside it.
Ask which of the three she heard. More than one answer is right -- all three are there.
If she misses one, play it again on Slower rather than translating it.
4.expected: The questions she heard, named by what they ask for: the name, the number of nights, breakfast. And two different voices.
4.support: Play it again on Slower, and again if she asks. Asking for a repeat is the content of this lesson -- do not take it away from her here.
4.challenge: Ask how she can tell that the voice changed.
4.monitoring: How many plays she needs, and whether she asks for them herself.
4.evidence: How many listenings she needed, and whether she asked for the repeat herself.
4.transition: Move on when she has answered both questions on screen.

5.goal: To connect each line at the desk with the information it gives or asks for, now with the lines written on screen.
run: The six lines are now on screen: the three she just heard, and three more from the same desk. This is the first screen on which she sees any of them written.
She says where each line goes; check the six together.
Talk only about the ones she got wrong.
Two CCQs: how many people spoke? (Two.) Did anybody ask for her passport? (No.)
5.expected: Each line placed under the name, the number of nights, or breakfast. The two that trip people up are the spelling question and the line about breakfast times -- neither is a question about her.
5.support: If she is stuck on a line, play the recording again on Slower before you explain anything.
5.challenge: Ask which of the six is not a question at all, and which of the two people said it.
5.monitoring: Whether she separates what is being asked from what is merely being said.
5.evidence: Whether seeing the lines changes what she understood on the first listening, and by how much.
5.transition: Move on when the six have been checked.

6.goal: For her to see, herself, which two reactions keep the conversation going.
run: Four reactions on screen. She chooses the two that keep the conversation going, and you check them together.
Then ask, in Portuguese if you need to: what happens after each one?
Let her name the difference before you do.
6.expected: In her own words: the two that ask for something keep the conversation going; smiling and saying she does not speak English give the desk nothing to answer, and it tends to end in gestures -- which is what already happens on her trips.
6.support: If she cannot say it, act out both endings -- one where you repeat, one where you switch to gestures -- and ask which one she wants.
6.challenge: Ask which of the two she would use first, and why.
6.monitoring: Whether she sees asking as a move, or as an admission.
6.evidence: How she describes what asking for a repeat means. It is the belief this lesson exists to change.
6.transition: Move on when she has named the difference.

7.goal: To get the five sentences said out loud, several times, and to have her ask for a repeat at least once without being told to.
7.interaction: T-S, live. Rounds, then out of order.
run: There is no audio on this screen: you ask the questions, she answers from the list.
Ask the three, one at a time. Then again, out of order.
ONCE, ask one of them at a faster pace. She has to ask you to repeat.
If she asks, say out loud that this was what the lesson wanted.
exact: The three questions, said slowly: "What is your name, please?" / "How many nights will you be staying?" / "Would you like breakfast?"
The fast one: ask one of the three at a naturally faster pace, without distorting the pronunciation.
When she asks for the repeat: "That. That is the lesson. You just did it."
If she freezes instead of asking, give the opening: "Sorry..."
7.expected: My name is... for the first, Four nights. for the second, Yes, please. or No, thank you. for the third -- and, on the fast one, Sorry, again please? or More slowly, please.
7.support: If she freezes instead of asking, give the first word of the repair sentence and wait.
7.challenge: Ask the three in a row without pausing, and let her sort them out.
7.monitoring: Whether the repair comes on its own, or only after you prompt it.
7.evidence: Whether she asked for a repeat without being told to, and on which question.
7.transition: Move on when she has asked for a repeat at least once, on her own.

8.goal: For her to hold the whole desk exchange live, and to repair once.
8.interaction: Role-play. You are the receptionist; she has just arrived.
run: Ask the three, one at a time. Say one of them faster.
The booking of lesson 1 is behind the Show the booking button. Open it if she asks for it, or if the dates escape her.
Do not correct during the role-play.
Write down what she says, as she says it. It is what the next lesson is planned from.
exact: Opening the desk: "Good afternoon. Checking in?"
The three, one at a time: "What is your name, please?" / "How many nights will you be staying?" / "Would you like breakfast?"
If she answers with a gesture: "In words, please."
8.expected: Three answers in words -- a short one such as Four nights. is a complete answer at a desk -- and one repair when the fast question arrives.
8.support: If she answers with a gesture, ask again and wait for words. If she asks for the booking, open it on screen.
8.challenge: Add a fourth question she has the language for: "And your booking number?"
8.monitoring: Whether the answer comes in words or stays a gesture, and whether the repair holds under pressure.
8.evidence: The three answers as she said them, and whether the repair happened without a prompt.
8.transition: Move on when the three have been answered.

9.goal: To write down one thing that worked and one to build on, and then to run the same three questions once more at a more natural pace.
9.interaction: T-S at the feedback board, then role-play again.
run: Fill in the board with her: what worked, one point to improve, and -- if there was one -- the first version of a sentence and a clearer version of it.
One point, not two.
Then open Replay and ask the three questions yourself, a little faster. One repeat allowed.
Do not add content here.
exact: Before the replay: "A little faster this time. You can stop me once -- choose your moment."
9.expected: The board filled in with her own words, and the three answered at the faster pace with the one repeat used.
9.support: If one repeat is not enough, allow a second and say so out loud. The number is not the point; using it is.
9.challenge: Run it with no repeat allowed and see what she does instead.
9.monitoring: Which question she spends her repeat on.
9.evidence: What went into the board, and where she chose to spend the repeat.
9.transition: Move on when the board is filled in and the replay has been done.

10.goal: To name what she did today, and to announce the next lesson.
10.interaction: T-S, with self-assessment by the student.
run: Read the list with her and mark what she recognizes. The Portuguese is under each line.
Say the homework out loud, and do not put it on screen: the post-class has the three questions written out and four free A1 resources.
Announce lesson 3 -- the verb she herself named in the consultation, to be.
Fill in the post-lesson record before you close.
exact: Announcing lesson 3: "You have already used this verb four times in two lessons. Next week we give it a name."
10.expected: Some of the items ticked, and one answer on the confidence row.
10.support: If she ticks nothing, read the list with her and ask which one she could use at a desk tomorrow.
10.challenge: Ask which of today's five sentences she would use first.
10.monitoring: Her reaction to the announcement about the verb.
10.evidence: Whether she asked for a repeat on her own during the lesson, and what she said when lesson 3 was announced.
